plan.title: Adipose treated vs control: variance partition + DE
plan.analytical_narrative:
The research question has two parts in order: first, how much of the per-gene expression variance is attributable to condition, sex, and age; second, which genes differ between treated and control. The inputs are a 12000 x 13 gene-level count CSV from Salmon (/data/inputs/counts/counts.csv, one gene-id column + 12 sample columns) and a 12 x 4 sample table (/data/inputs/metadata/metadata.csv) carrying condition (treated/control, 6 vs 6), sex (F/M) and age (years). Design is unpaired, single batch, human adipose.

T1S1 does the sample-structure QC that every count dataset needs before a model: blind VST, PCA on the top 500 variable genes coloured by condition and sex, sample-distance heatmap, library sizes. This is the check that no sample is an outlier and that condition, not sex, drives the leading axis.

T1S4 answers the first half of the question directly: a variancePartition mixed model per gene on voom log-CPM with precision weights, condition and sex as random effects (categorical), age as a fixed effect (continuous), reporting the distribution of variance fractions across genes plus the residual. This is a design diagnostic, run before the test and independently of it — it is descriptive and cannot license a claim about which genes differ.

T1S2 answers the second half: DESeq2 with design ~ sex + age_centered + condition, condition reference level set explicitly to control, Wald test on the condition_treated_vs_control coefficient, apeglm shrinkage, BH at alpha 0.05 with independent filtering on. Covariates enter the design as terms — they are not regressed out of the counts. With 6 per group, sex adjustment costs 1 df and age 1 df; the step must report the design matrix rank and confirm sex is not confounded with condition, because with 12 samples a badly unbalanced sex split would make the condition coefficient unstable. edgeR quasi-likelihood is run on the same design as the robustness second method and the intersection reported as the high-confidence set.

A caveat that constrains the whole plan: the counts are a gene-level Salmon table and the profile explicitly does not say whether the length correction was applied. There are no per-sample quant.sf files and no average-transcript-length table in the inputs, so the length offset cannot be reconstructed. The model is therefore fitted on the counts as delivered with no length offset, and both T1S2 and T1S3 must state that a shift in isoform usage can appear as differential expression. tximport is not run — it imports transcript-level estimates and cannot be applied to a gene table.

T1S3 assembles the report: variance fractions, MA and dispersion plots, p-value histogram, effect table with unshrunken and shrunken log2FC plus lfcSE ranked by the shrunken value, the DESeq2/edgeR overlap, and the reproducibility record. No enrichment step is planned — the question does not ask for pathways.

flags.message: A quantifier name alone does not establish that the length correction occurred. If the counts come from Salmon, kallisto, or RSEM as a gene-level table, with no per-sample quantification files and no average transcript length table, the import state is not established. Ask for the per-sample quantification files, quant.sf, abundance.h5, or genes.results, or for the average transcript length table per gene and sample. If neither arrives, fit the count model on the counts as delivered, with no length offset, and state in the plan and in the report that the length offset is lost and that a change in isoform use can show as differential expression. Do not run tximport on a gene table, because tximport imports transcript estimates, and do not invent a length input.
